title: Contains Duplicate
description: Stream once; the first repeated value short-circuits to true. Set membership is O(1).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given an array `nums` and I need to return `true` if any value appears at least twice, `false` if every value is distinct. A couple of quick questions before I code:"

• What are the elements — integers only, or could there be strings or mixed types?
• Any size bound on the array? Anything I should worry about for memory?
• Are NaN or `-0`/`+0` in play? (Set treats `NaN` as equal to itself, but `===` doesn't — worth flagging.)
• Empty input — return `false`, right?
sections.why: The element-type question matters because Set uses SameValueZero equality, which differs from `===` on exactly one edge: `NaN`. If the interviewer says "floats are possible," you've now planted a flag that the Set behavior is intentional rather than accidental. The empty-input check is a 5-second clarification that prevents a silly miss at the end.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is two nested loops: outer `i` from 0, inner `j` from `i+1`, check `nums[i] === nums[j]`. First match returns `true`. That's O(n²) time, O(1) extra space — let me see if we can trade some space for time."

"There's also a sort-then-scan-adjacent variant — O(n log n) time, but it mutates the input array, and the default `.sort()` is lexicographic which would order `[1,10,2]` wrong without a comparator. I'd flag both before I went that direction."
sections.why: Naming both brute forces — nested loops AND sort — is more thorough than just one. It shows you considered the alternatives. The lexicographic-sort gotcha is the kind of trivia interviewers respect: it proves you've actually been burned by `[1,10,2].sort()` returning `[1,10,2]` and know to reach for a numeric comparator.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to a hash set?
sections.say: "This is the canonical Set-membership problem. The signal: for each element I'm asking 'have I seen this before?' — that's O(1) membership lookup, and I don't need any value associated with the key, just presence. Set gives me exactly that. I'll walk the array once, and for each element check `seen.has(n)` BEFORE adding it. First hit returns `true`; if I finish the loop, return `false`."
sections.why: Naming the data structure AND the structural property — 'O(1) membership, no associated value needed' — is what distinguishes derivation from guessing. If the problem had asked 'count duplicates' I'd reach for a Map (need a count). If it had asked 'find the first index that repeats' I'd still want a Set, but storing the index. Spelling out which property unlocks Set is what the interviewer is grading.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me run a couple of inputs through the model." Three cases — a typical dup-found-mid-array, an all-unique case that walks the full loop, and an all-same case that returns on the second element.

examples.note: Typical case — duplicate is the very last element.
All unique — loop runs to completion and falls through to the trailing `return false`.
All-same — short-circuits on the second element. The check-before-add order is what prevents the first 1 from matching itself.
examples.trace:
n=1 → seen.has(1)=false (we DON'T match ourselves) → seen={1}
n=1 → seen.has(1)=true! return true ✓

sections.why: The all-same case is the one to mention out loud — it's why the order is `check → add`, not `add → check`. If you added first, the very first 1 would 'find' itself on the next has-check (or worse, on the same iteration if you wrote it inline). The all-unique trace also defends the worst-case bound: even when the answer is false, we only walk the array once.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Empty array → loop doesn't fire, returns `false` (vacuously: no duplicates exist).
• One element → same — no duplicate is possible.
• Mixed types like `[1, '1']` → `===` and Set's SameValueZero treat these as distinct, so this returns `false`. That might or might not be the intended behavior — worth asking.
• `NaN` in the array → Set treats `NaN === NaN` for membership, even though `NaN !== NaN` under `===`. So `[NaN, NaN]` returns `true`, which is actually the *intuitive* answer.
• Very large array of all-unique → O(n) memory in the Set. If memory's a constraint and we accept O(n log n) time, sort-and-scan in place is the alternative.
sections.why: The NaN call-out is the senior-tier touch — most candidates don't know that Set and Map use SameValueZero rather than `===`. If the interviewer asks 'why does that matter,' you've got an answer ready: it's the one place Set's equality differs from `===`. The memory-vs-time tradeoff at the end shows you understand this is a deliberate engineering choice, not a default.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — one pass, with O(1) `has` and `add` per element. The short-circuit on first match can return early, but the worst case is all-unique, which still walks the whole array.

Space is O(n) — the Set holds at most n entries in the worst case (all-unique).

If you wanted to extend this: 'Contains Duplicate II' adds a constraint — duplicates must be within distance k of each other. The fix is to switch from Set to a sliding window of size k (still O(n)). The template here — Set-as-membership — is the building block; the windowed variant just bounds the Set's lifetime."
sections.why: The amortization story is straightforward — one pass, O(1) per element — but the wrap-up's job is to show transfer. Naming Contains Duplicate II unprompted is the move that proves you see this as a *template* (Set-for-membership) rather than a one-off. Interviewers grade transfer heavily because it predicts how you'll handle the variant they'll throw at you on the follow-up.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical Contains Duplicate one statement at a time on a real input. The highlighted line is what just ran; the state panel shows the locals after that step. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}`, state: { nums } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'init seen (empty Set)', state: { nums, seen: [] } };
yield { line: 3, label: `outer step: i=${i}, n=${n}`, state: { nums, seen: [...seen], i, n } };
yield { line: 5, label: `seen.has(${n}) → true — duplicate found, short-circuit`, state: { nums, seen: [...seen], i, n, returns: true } };
yield { line: 5, label: `seen.has(${n}) → false (no duplicate yet)`, state: { nums, seen: [...seen], i, n } };
yield { line: 6, label: `seen.add(${n})`, state: { nums, seen: [...seen], i, n } };
yield { line: 8, label: 'loop ended without finding a duplicate — return false', state: { nums, seen: [...seen], returns: false } };

notes: Check has BEFORE add — otherwise every element would falsely match itself.
Set.has is O(1) average; sorting + scan would be O(n log n) and unnecessary.
Short-circuit on the first duplicate — no need to keep counting.

options: To avoid matching the element with itself
It is faster than the reverse order
questions.explain: If you add first, every element finds itself in the Set on the very next check.

questions.q: Space complexity in the worst case (all unique)?
Why prefer a Set over sorting + scanning adjacent pairs?
options: Set gives O(n) instead of O(n log n)
Sort needs a custom numeric comparator (default sort is lexicographic — [1,10,2])
Both the mutation and the asymptotic reasons
questions.explain: Set is asymptotically faster AND avoids mutating the caller array. The comparator gotcha is real but tangential to dedup correctness.

questions.q: What is the one-liner `return new Set(nums).size !== nums.length` doing?
options: Checking if the array is sorted
If dedup shrank the count, some value repeated — so a duplicate exists
Counting how many duplicates there are
questions.explain: Building a Set drops repeats; if its size is smaller than the array length, at least one value collapsed, meaning there was a duplicate.

questions.q: What does the canonical return on an empty array []?
questions.explain: The loop body never runs, so control falls through to the trailing `return false` — no values means no duplicates, which is vacuously correct.

questions.q: Why does the early `return true` on the first duplicate not change the worst-case time complexity?
options: Early return makes it O(log n)
The worst case is all-unique input, where no early exit fires and the full array is scanned
questions.explain: Short-circuiting only helps when a dup appears early; the worst case (all distinct) still walks every element, so the bound stays O(n).

questions.q: The brute-force nested-loop version is O(n²). What does the Set buy in exchange for its O(n) space?
options: Nothing — it is the same speed
It replaces the O(n) inner membership scan with an O(1) Set lookup, dropping time to O(n)
questions.explain: Brute force re-scans seen elements (O(n)) for each item; the Set answers 'have I seen this?' in O(1), trading O(n) memory for O(n) total time.
